#7735. "Would 'Go Luigi'" Was a Threat, and Thus Subject to Harassment Prevention Order Statute

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From D.M. v. A.M., decided by Massachusetts Appellate Court Justices Ariane Vuono, William Meade & Zachary Hillman on Oct. 21:

The defendant, A.M., appeals from the extension of a harassment prevention order …..

To review a civil harassment prevention order, "we consider whether the judge could find, by a preponderance of the evidence, together with all permissible inferences, that the defendant committed acts that constituted one of the enumerated forms of harassment." As relevant here, "[h]arassment" is defined as "[three] or more acts of willful and malicious conduct aimed at a specific person committed with the intent to cause fear, intimidation, [or] abuse." To qualify, the conduct must be intended to cause and actually cause fear of physical harm or damage to property….

Here, as the District Court judge properly found, there were three or more incidents constituting harassment. On June 27, 2025, the defendant called the Target store that D.M. managed, looking for D.M., and became vulgar with the employees when she was told that D.M. was not there.

On June 28, 2025, the defendant showed up at the Target store and demanded to speak to D.M. The defendant then called Target's customer service line and made multiple threats, including that she would "go Luigi" and that she was "at the point of feeling like Luigi" and that D.M. was "gonna be sorry though."

On June 30, 2025, the defendant called Target again, looking for D.M., and stated, "this is why people go full Luigi." {The judge noted, and we agree, that the defendant was referencing Luigi Mangione, who at the time was accused of murdering Brian Thompson, the Chief Executive Officer of UnitedHealthcare.}

On July 1, 2025, the defendant called again and stated that she would continue calling and coming to the store looking for D.M. The judge properly found that these events constituted three or more incidents of harassment ….

The defendant's repeated calls and trips to the Target store and her references to Luigi Mangione reasonably support an inference that she intended to cause D.M. fear, intimidation, or abuse. Additionally, as the judge properly found, D.M. was "petrified" from these threats, moving to work at a different location to avoid the defendant. Therefore, the judge did not err in extending the harassment prevention order….

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 3, 1845

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7734. What Happened to Cheap, Basic Cars?

"Feature creep" has left cars over-expensive and stuffed with technology. Is it even possible to go back to basics?

There was a time when buying a cheap new car was relatively simple. The answer might have involved crank windows, manual door locks, an AM/FM radio, and seats upholstered in something that looked suspiciously like industrial carpeting.

Today, the idea of a truly low-budget, no-frills vehicle is getting hard to find. Even the least expensive new cars come with touchscreens, driver-assistance systems, connectivity features, multiple airbags, and enough electronic wizardry to make a 1990s luxury car look like a farm tractor by comparison.

That raises a reasonable question: Can you still buy a genuinely inexpensive, basic vehicle in 2026? The short answer is yes, but “basic” no longer means what it used to.

Before we talk about what no-frills, low-budget vehicles are available, it’s important that we set a baseline for what that kind of car is in today’s market.

Modern safety and fuel economy technology are two of the biggest reasons today’s inexpensive vehicles don’t look anything like their ancestors. A new car sold in the United States must meet extensive federal safety requirements. That means airbags, stability control, rearview backup cameras, crash protection, and a long list of other requirements.

Consumers have also developed expectations. Try selling a new car without air conditioning today and see how quickly the internet catches fire. Nobody wants to return to the days when a buyer had to choose between air conditioning and an AM/FM radio. Budget buyers today expect power windows, remote locks, smartphone connectivity, and decent climate control.

The result is an interesting middle ground. Today’s cheapest cars aren’t truly bare-bones. Automakers have figured out how to put a surprising amount of technology into relatively inexpensive vehicles without necessarily making them luxury cars.

For years, the sub-$20,000 new car was the entry point for budget-conscious buyers. Models like the Mitsubishi Mirage, Nissan Versa, Chevrolet Spark, and various tiny hatchbacks gave shoppers an inexpensive way into a new vehicle.

Many of those cars are gone now. The market has steadily moved toward larger vehicles, more equipment, higher prices, and greater complexity. That doesn’t mean inexpensive cars have disappeared. It means the definition of inexpensive has moved upward. A buyer looking for a new vehicle in the low-$20,000 range can still find options, but those vehicles aren’t exactly stripped-down A-to-B appliances anymore.

Even inexpensive cars now tend to have infotainment screens, Bluetooth, backup cameras, automatic emergency braking, lane-departure warnings, and other features that were once the exclusive territory of expensive luxury models.

The economy in the U.S. has changed significantly. Not just from COVID and various political changes, but also from the general mindset of most Americans. When we compare pricing from 30 or even just 15 years ago, we often mentally skew the results due to our perspective of that change. It’s important to remember that, thanks to inflation, a dollar from 2011 is not a dollar in 2026. That ‘11 dollar is now $1.49. Inflation compounds and that 15 years has meant a 49 percent decrease in value for our money.

Knowing that, we can compare the average new vehicle purchase price (currently about $51,000) today with the average 15 years ago ($30,500). Then we can compare those values to the average household income from both eras: $50,000 in 2011 and $87,500 in 2026. Doing that, we find that things haven’t changed much.

The average new vehicle price seems very high compared to 15 years ago, but it was about 60 percent of the average household income in 2011 and is still that for 2026.

Yes and no. If your definition of low-budget means “I need reliable transportation and I don’t care whether it has the latest technology,” the used market is still where you’ll get a good deal. But a good deal doesn’t always mean good value. Shopping for a used vehicle is a whole discussion unto itself and countless books, videos, and articles have been made detailing the do’s and don’ts.

What’s important and relevant here is to realize that while a three- to seven-year-old compact car can provide much of the transportation value that new economy cars once offered, it will come with some downsides. The trick is to shop based on condition and ownership history rather than simply finding the cheapest four-door vehicle.

What’s more, the used car market has changed significantly since the COVID blip. Up until just before the shutdowns began, the used car market remained relatively steady in pricing versus the new car market, with long-term changes largely following inflation. During COVID, used car prices jumped by about 49 percent as demand for vehicles collided with a lack of new vehicles due to closures. Afterward, as new cars began to once again appear on dealership lots, the used car market eventually saw less demand and adjusted accordingly.

That adjustment, however, wasn’t back down to pre-COVID numbers. It’s still 17 percent higher than it was. And it seems to have decided to hold steady there. The reason used cars are much more expensive is, again, supply and demand. This time between used car availability and demand from buyers wanting them. There are fewer used cars being sold because owners are keeping their used cars longer. This disparity and its higher price result has been a big driver in new car sales for the past few years.

Yes, but you have to adjust your expectations. If your definition of “no-frills” is “nothing I don’t need,” the new-car market still has possibilities. If your definition is “give me an engine, four wheels, a steering wheel, and absolutely nothing else,” you’re probably shopping used or waiting on the upcoming Slate pickup truck.

For now, here are the five lowest-cost new vehicles you can buy in 2026, ranked by base model price tag and not including shipping and destination charges:

#7731. What’s Downshifting? The Trend That’s Helping Homeowners Do More With Less

Downshifting can mean a smaller home, fewer belongings, or a lighter schedule. Here's how the lifestyle works and where to start.

Sometimes less IS more. At least, that’s what one home and lifestyle trend would have you believe.

A house can demand more time and money than homeowners expect. Spare bedrooms fill up with things nobody uses, the yard needs another afternoon of work, and there’s always something that needs fixing. Downshifting is one way homeowners are trying to change that.

Here’s what downshifting means, how it’s different from downsizing, and whether it can actually save money.

A post shared by RetroSuburbia (@retrosuburbiaofficial)

Downshifting is pretty much what it sounds like. It’s a decision to slow things down a bit, spend less, and get rid of some of the things that take up too much time or space around the house.

Permaculture writer David Holmgren covers the idea in his book RetroSuburbia, which describes downshifting as “a conscious choice and action to shift to a lifestyle with less consumption, complexity, stress and status seeking.” The idea is to make everyday life a little easier to manage, whether that’s by cutting expenses or having fewer responsibilities.

It sounds a lot like downsizing, but the two aren’t quite the same. Downsizing usually means moving to a smaller house or getting rid of belongings. Downshifting doesn’t necessarily involve moving at all.

One family might trade a large house for a smaller place that needs less maintenance. Another might stay right where they are, stop buying things they don’t need, or spend less time working on the house.

Homeowners can start by looking at what’s taking up the most time or money. Maybe that’s a garage full of things that haven’t been used in years, or a spare bedroom that’s become a storage room. Clearing out those spaces can mean less to clean and look after.

Other changes can be pretty small, too. Borrowing a tool instead of buying one, fixing furniture rather than replacing it, or starting a small vegetable garden are all examples. The Environmental Protection Agency also recommends buying less and reusing things to help reduce waste.

Even looking for ways to lower utility bills, like sealing drafty windows or keeping up with heating and cooling maintenance, can be part of downshifting.

One reason people consider downshifting is to save money. Buying fewer things and using less energy can certainly help, but moving to a smaller home doesn’t automatically mean smaller bills.

“New homeowners are often surprised by the costs of owning property,” according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The agency recommends putting together a budget that includes property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other expenses beyond the mortgage.

There are some practical things to consider, too. A smaller house might not have enough room for a growing family, and moving farther away could mean a longer commute. Even growing vegetables or repairing things around the house takes time.

Still, for some households, having fewer things to pay for and maintain can leave more time for family, hobbies, or just enjoying the house they already have.

And that’s really the point of downshifting. It doesn’t have to mean selling a house or getting rid of everything. Sometimes it’s as simple as deciding the house doesn’t need another project or another piece of furniture.

Does your home’s landscape look barren and brown after autumn leaves fall, and doesn’t perk back up again until spring? Furnace and air conditioner filters are integral to the ongoing operation of the HVAC system, so it’s important to find out what you might not know about HVAC air filters. Learning more about air filters for furnace filtration can help you determine what to look for when choosing a furnace filter’s replacement, including the type of air filter and MERV rating, as well as furnace and air conditioner filter sizes.

Before picking up the first air filter you find, it’s a good idea to determine which type of air filter is best for the home and existing HVAC system. Even the best HVAC brands typically offer a variety of air filter options to choose from, so it’s recommended to learn more about home air conditioner filters, including washable, disposable, fiberglass, pleated, electrostatic, and polyester air filters.

Even the best energy-efficient air conditioners will suffer if they are not equipped with an appropriate air filter. Deciding on the right air filter can be difficult, though, without understanding the terms used to measure the filtration quality and efficiency. MERV stands for minimum efficiency reporting value, which is a number assigned to a product based on its density and filtration capabilities.

Andrew Hulsebos, service director for Reiner Group, a heating and air conditioning company in northern New Jersey, says that the MERV rating system ranges from 1 to 20, and that higher numbers indicate a higher level of filtration. “For residential use, air filters are typically rated between MERV 5 to 13.” Higher-efficiency filters are mainly used in commercial settings or health facilities that are equipped with powerful HVAC systems that are capable of drawing the air through the dense filters.

Furnace and AC air filters are available in a wide range of sizes and thicknesses, so it’s necessary to check the HVAC system operating manual to determine the right size for your system. Generally, if the filter needs to be bent, jammed, or otherwise forced into position, it’s too big. Similarly, the air filter may be too small if it doesn’t come within an inch of all four corners of the air handler slot or frame.

The easiest way to determine the right size air filter for the home is to check the existing air filter. The measurements are usually listed on the frame of the filter, making it easy to find the size. Alternatively, you can measure the existing air filter with a tape measure, or even measure the air intake slot to find out the appropriate size air filter for the HVAC system.

Homeowners will want to stay on top of a range of maintenance tasks to keep the home functional and comfortable, but knowing exactly what needs to be done isn’t always obvious. Before purchasing replacement air filters for furnaces and home AC, it’s worth checking out the answers below to some of the most frequently asked questions about HVAC air filters.

Yes, furnaces and AC units generally use the same air filter. “They share the same air handler, where the filter is located, which means you don’t need to worry about buying separate filters for each system,” says Hulsebos.

Yes. The most common HVAC configuration for residential properties typically involves the furnace and air conditioner sharing the same air filter, so to properly maintain the air conditioner, the furnace filter will need to be replaced or washed when necessary. How often to replace an air filter depends on the number of people and pets, and the frequency with which the home is used. On average, though, you should replace the filter about every 3 months.

The number of air filters in a house tends to depend on the size of the home, including the square footage, number of floors, and the number of HVAC units. Generally, a single air filter is enough for most residential properties, though larger homes may have more than one HVAC unit, each requiring at least one air filter.

HEPA air filters are often considered high-quality products with excellent filtration capabilities. However, Hulsebos notes that “part of the reason that HEPA filters are so rarely used in HVAC systems is that they are extremely restrictive in terms of airflow.” HEPA filters can also be expensive, difficult to clean, and typically need to be replaced every 6 to 12 months.

Residential HVAC systems usually require a filter with a MERV rating between 5 and 13. Air filters with higher MERV ratings may be able to filter smaller particles, but they may put unnecessary stress on the HVAC system as the blower attempts to force the air through the dense filter. So while a higher MERV rating can be better, the air filter needs to be paired with a suitable HVAC system for optimal performance.

Generally, the maximum MERV rating for a residential furnace is 13, though commercial or health care facilities may have more powerful HVAC systems that can operate normally while using air filters up to MERV 20.

The most commonly used air filter in an HVAC system is a pleated air filter. This is because it has high filtration capabilities and a relatively low price. These air filters can generally be purchased online or from a local home improvement store, though some grocery stores may also carry pleated air filters.

#7728. City's Using Meta Moderation Assist Feature for Facebook Comments Doesn't Violate First Amendment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Ruth Bermudez Montenegro (S.D. Cal.) Oct. 22 in Jalisi v. City of Poway:

The City of Poway … maintains a public Facebook page where it "posts updates about various items that may be of interest to [City] residents and the general public." The Facebook page is open to public comment, and members of the public routinely comment on posts on the page. Plaintiff is a resident of Poway who has criticized aspects of the City's decisions for several years, including by speaking during city council meetings, corresponding with City officials, and posting critical comments on the City's Facebook page. City officials and staff, including those responsible for the Facebook page, appear to recognize Plaintiff as a critic.

Several times during the past year, Plaintiff's comments on the City's Facebook page have been "hidden" or "shadow banned;" that is, his comments are not deleted and are still visible when Plaintiff looks at the posts, but are not visible when other Facebook users look at the posts. The City's Social Media Policy provides that "[t]he City's social media presence serves as a limited public forum and all content shall be monitored and moderated." The Policy indicates that user-generated posts will be deleted if those posts, among other things: "use[ ] abusive, vulgar, offensive, profane, sexual, threatening, deliberately untruthful or defamatory language or content." Additionally, "[p]ostings from a public user account which contain inappropriate or disruptive content, … or believed to be spam, may result in the public user account being blocked from any further activity on the City's social media account … at the discretion of the City Manager's Office."

Plaintiff believes that the City is hiding his comments because it wants to suppress his critical viewpoints…. The City represents that none of its employees have ever hidden or removed any comments made by Plaintiff; instead, Meta's Moderation Assist Program has hidden these comments because it has flagged Plaintiff's Facebook profile as a "non-human 'bot'" account. Meta Moderation Assist "is necessary because the City does not have the resources nor ability to actively monitor each and every comment made in real time in order to manually hide bot comments, particularly considering these comments can be submitted 24 hours a day seven days a week." The City believes that Plaintiff's comments were hidden because Moderation Assist flagged him as a bot: "Moderation Assist will automatically hide a post if (1) the commenter does not have any friends or followers, (2) the comment has a link, or (3) the commenter does not have a profile picture." Plaintiff does not have a profile picture, has only one Facebook friend, and has no posts on his own profile, which "are typically strong indicators that the account is a non-human bot."

The city agreed that viewpoint-based moderation of Jalisi's posts would be unconstitutional, and agreed to "… manually unhiding Plaintiff's prior Facebook posts." But it opposed Plaintiff's request to "remove any restriction that causes Plaintiff's comments on the City Page to be hidden from the public"; it argued that it needed to keep using the Moderation Assist program, and couldn't turn it off only for Jalisi. And the court held in favor of the city as to this:

[T]he Court need decide whether the City's Facebook page is a limited public forum or a designated public forum. Even when considering laws regulating expression in "quintessential public forums," courts "ask first whether the law is content based or content neutral." …

As a threshold matter, based on the limited and preliminary record before it, the Court notes it is likely that Plaintiff's comments were hidden not by a City policy, but by the Meta Moderation Assist Program. But even assuming … that the restrictive effects of the Meta Moderation Assist Program may be attributed to the City, the Court does not find the restrictions unconstitutional.

First, the restriction is facially content neutral. Based on the Carmichael Declaration, profiles are not flagged as bots by "examin[ing] the content of the message that is conveyed." Rather, they are flagged based on the presence of certain predictive factors, such as the absence of a profile picture or the absence of other Facebook friends. Thus, determining whether a comment may be hidden has nothing to do with the content of the comment.

Second, the restriction can be "justified without reference to the content of the regulated speech" and there is no sign that the restriction was "adopted by the government because of disagreement with the message [the speech] conveys." The City uses Meta Moderation Assist because it "does not have the resources nor ability to actively monitor each and every comment made in real time in order to manually hide bot comments." There is nothing in the record to suggest that the City turned to Meta Moderation Assist "motivated by disagreement with any particular expressive" conduct. Indeed, Plaintiff's evidence that identical comments published by other users remained visible actually strengthens the finding that the restriction is content neutral; critical speech is clearly tolerated by the City. Therefore, the Court finds that the restriction is content neutral and applies intermediate scrutiny.

To survive intermediate scrutiny, the restriction must "'further[ ] an important or substantial governmental interest,' that interest must be 'unrelated to the suppression of free expression,' and the 'incidental restriction on alleged First Amendment freedoms [must be] no greater than is essential to the furtherance of that interest.'"

The City asserts that its interest in using Meta Moderation Assist is "prevent[ing] non-human 'bot' spam postings on its Facebook page, which can overwhelm public pages and make it much more difficult for the public to both obtain important information and participate in the conversation." The Court finds that the two-way exchange of information between the citizenry and the City is a substantial governmental interest.

Furthermore, that interest is "unrelated to the suppression of free expression." In fact, the interest runs counter to the suppression of free expression; it seeks to ensure that residents have effective access to the exchange of ideas with their neighbors and their government. The interest is related to the suppression of expression by non-human bots, but bots are neither "human beings with First Amendment rights" nor the "[corporations] … composed of [them … that] possess First Amendment rights themselves."

Finally, although the record shows there are "incidental restriction[s]" on speech, such as the hiding of comments posted by human beings flagged as bots, those "incidental restriction[s]" are "no greater than essential to the furtherance" of the governmental interest here. "A critical feature of this inquiry turns on whether the [government] seriously undertook to address the problems it faces with less intrusive tools readily available to it." Again, on the early record before it, the Court finds that the City has no alternative methods to prevent non-human bot accounts from flooding their Facebook page. This is not a situation where there is an obvious, alternative method of regulation that would achieve the governmental interest and incidentally censor no speech….

Alan B. Fenstermacher and Jayson A. Parsons (Rutan & Tucker) represent the City.

#7727. Airbnb Just Did Something Guests Have Been Asking for Years — Here’s What Changed

Airbnb is putting limits on checkout chores, including washing dishes and stripping beds. Here's what hosts can still ask guests to do.

Everyone loves a vacation. But the cleanup and tidying as the trip is finishing up? Not so much.

It’s not always clear what guests are responsible for cleaning. Dishes, sheets, towels, and taking out the trash are sometimes part of checkout instructions at Airbnb rentals. With checkout typically at 11 a.m., the last morning of a trip can turn into a mad dash through an unreasonably long chore list, even when a cleaning fee has been tacked onto the bill.

That frustration, along with a growing number of travelers returning to hotels for more consistent quality and fees, is behind Airbnb’s new checkout rules. Learn which tasks guests may still face, and how hosts are responding.

Starting with reservations booked on or after November 20, 2026, Airbnb will require hosts to clearly explain their house rules and checkout requests before guests book. Hosts won’t be allowed to add new requirements through messages or signs inside the rental after a reservation is confirmed.

“House Rules are now displayed more prominently on your listing, where guests can easily see them before they book,” according to Airbnb’s announcement. Guests can also find these instructions in their Trips tab and reservation reminders.

Under the new policy, hosts generally can’t require guests to strip beds, start laundry, wash and put away dishes, or take trash to an off-site disposal facility. However, hosts can still request simpler tasks, such as placing dirty dishes in the sink, gathering used towels, or putting trash and recycling in designated bins. Guests may also be asked to turn off lights and return keys before leaving.

Airbnb’s policy distinguishes between house rules and requests. “Guests must follow hosts’ house rules, and are encouraged to comply with hosts’ requests,” according to the company. Some exceptions may apply. For example, rentals in areas with bears may require guests to use animal-proof trash containers, while drought restrictions could affect water use.

Guests are still responsible for leaving the property reasonably tidy. Airbnb’s ground rules for guests prohibit excessive messes and require guests to take responsibility for damage beyond normal wear and tear. Hosts can still charge standard cleaning fees and request reimbursement for unexpected cleaning costs or damage.

Hosts who don’t follow Airbnb’s new checkout rules could receive warnings or requests to update their listings. Repeated violations may lead to notices on their listings or lower placement in search results. Hosts can also appeal flagged requests.

The policy also prevents hosts from charging their own fines for missed chores or restricting access to amenities already included in a reservation.

However, not every host supports the changes. Some believe washing dishes after cooking is a reasonable responsibility for guests, while others worry the new rules could increase cleaning costs. A Change.org petition has called on Airbnb to reverse its restrictions on requiring guests to wash dishes.

Guests who encounter unexpected chores or requests that violate the new policy can contact Airbnb for help.

#7726. The Best Salt Spreaders of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Updated Nov 3, 2026 8:55 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Salt spreaders don’t get the attention they deserve. Though freshly fallen snow has a beautiful way of blanketing neighborhoods in a peaceful ambiance, it’s not long before cold concrete can turn that snow into slippery ice. Enter salt spreaders, which are simple tools that make it much easier and quicker to apply deicing salt to driveways, walkways, and other outdoor areas.

Though I’m a firm believer in safety first, I also acknowledge that using too much salt to melt accumulated snow and ice can damage concrete, harm plants and animals, and contaminate water. Salt spreaders help mitigate this problem by maintaining even distribution and keeping salt confined to intended areas.

To determine which salt spreaders are worth their price, we researched dozens of popular spreaders before testing six top options on our driveway and walkways, as well as on our front steps and deck. Our favorite was the Scotts Elite Spreader for its even and easy application, convenience and control, and ability to accommodate both granular and rock salt. Read on to see our test results for this and the rest of the products we recommend before choosing one of the best salt spreaders for your property.

Bottom line: Salt spreaders are essential for safe, efficient deicing. The Scotts Elite Spreader stands out, but other models offer great alternatives for various needs.

Our Ratings: Assembly 5/5; Distribution 4.75/5; Durability 4.5/5; Value 5/5

With a dual-rotor design, the Scotts Elite walk-behind salt spreader has an impressive 80-pound capacity and 6-foot spread width for quick salt application to driveways, sidewalks, and decks. It comes mostly assembled, other than attaching its 10-inch never-flat tires and flipping up its ergonomic handle. In our tests, we found it stable and easy to maneuver, even when filled with all 35 pounds of ice melt we had on hand.

The Scotts Elite salt dispenser for snow and ice features dial settings from two to 15, meaning it works with everything from fine lawn fertilizers to chunky rock salt. Since we’re careful to avoid unnecessarily applying ice melt for environmental and economic reasons, we wish this model featured its EdgeGuard technology next to both rotors instead of just one. Still, so long as we planned which direction we went when working next to our lawn, we found the application to be even and relatively easy to control.

What our tester says: “If I could only choose one salt and fertilizer spreader, this would be it. It holds a ton of product, moves easily over uneven terrain, and makes quick work of large areas.” —Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Scotts Elite salt spreader at Tractor Supply Co., Ace Hardware, or The Home Depot.

While we were happy to melt ice and snow with the help of our top pick, we understand that it may not be right for everyone. The following five spreaders also passed our tests and might be better for those with differing capacity needs.

There are hundreds of salt spreaders on the market, so choosing just a few to test wasn’t easy. To make our decision, we researched various types of spreaders, including everything from salt spreaders for trucks to simple feed scoops. Once we selected six options, we put each through a series of tests, including assembly, using them with granular salt and rock salt, and evaluating any additional features. We rated each product according to a rubric and gave the highest overall scorer our award for the best salt spreader.

When choosing the right salt spreader, there are a few important factors to keep in mind. These include the size of the surfaces in need of salting, which type of spreader you prefer, and the quality of materials, among other things.

The snow salt spreaders we tested for home use are exclusively walk-behind and handheld models. However, larger commercial settings may require a truck salt spreader or a salt spreader for a tractor.

Many residential salt spreaders are designed as compact handheld units. Scoop-style models are sometimes fully open, and others have lids with various-size holes to accommodate both granular and rock salt while helping control the amount of product dispensed at once.

A slightly more complex handheld salt spreader may feature a hopper up top and a mechanism that opens to allow salt to project from the front of the spreader. Open-top hopper-style units are available in hand-crank or battery-powered versions with dials to allow various sizes of ice through. These types of handheld units generally work best with granular salt and may clog with rock-style products.

Walk-behind salt spreaders are more substantial than handheld units, incorporating larger hoppers as well as wheels, handles, and a range of additional features. They’re better suited to larger surfaces where users want to cover a decent amount of square footage quickly. On the flip side, their size makes them tricky to use in tight spots and on stairs.

Our top picks for walk-behind spreaders project salt in widths between 4 and 6 feet and feature at least one fin or deflector to help control spread width as desired. Most walk-behind spreaders have a wide range of opening settings to accommodate small materials like fertilizer, substantial pieces of rock salt, and everything in between.

While we only tested handheld and walk-behind spreaders in this guide, towable and hitch-mount salt spreaders are also available for larger properties or commercial use. Towable electric salt spreaders can help users avoid having to rely on snow removal services for the job, although they do require mounting to a truck, ATV, or lawn tractor.

Perhaps the biggest factor to consider when choosing the best salt spreader is the size of the area in need of treatment before or after a storm. Since handheld units often hold only 5 pounds of salt or less, they’re better for smaller spaces like stairs or detailed work alongside the edge of a driveway.

Walk-behind units are helpful for driveways, sidewalks, and decks since they allow quick application over larger areas and often incorporate fins or deflectors to help increase accuracy. The walk-behind units we tested have a capacity of 80 to 130 pounds, though smaller and larger models are available. In our perfect world, we would own both a walk-behind and a handheld spreader for speed and precision.

Towable salt spreaders can hold over 100 pounds of salt, making them ideal for deicing sizable surfaces quickly. Generally speaking, though, they aren’t as accurate as smaller units.

Most salt spreaders are made with plastic hoppers since the material is lightweight, relatively durable, and easy to maintain. Steel or stainless steel salt spreaders may be more durable over the years, but they generally weigh more and will require additional maintenance to prevent rust.

Salt spreader handles and broadcast plates may also be made of either metal or plastic. As with the hopper, the use of metal in these parts may make them more durable but also heavier and in need of additional maintenance.

While the above sections cover the most important features of salt spreaders, you may still have a few questions if you’ve never used one. Below, we answer a few of the most common queries about these devices.

Salt spreaders are an efficient and affordable way to reduce the time and effort it takes to keep potentially slippery surfaces safe in winter. They can also help save on snow removal costs. We think they are worth it, especially if you live anywhere snowfall is a relatively common occurrence.

Many fertilizer spreaders work with salt, provided the salt is small and granular. If the opening is big enough, your current fertilizer spreader may even accommodate rock salt. If you don’t have a salt spreader but need to melt ice, our guide on how to melt ice without salt provides a few additional methods.

Yes, the best time to spread salt is before it snows. Salting an hour or more before a snowfall helps prevent snow from sticking. If you miss your window to salt before a storm, be sure to use a snow shovel to clear as much accumulation as possible before applying salt using a spreader.

There are two reasons why it’s far from ideal to leave salt in a salt spreader. First, salt is corrosive and can damage your spreader over time. Second, if moisture from the air or wayward rain or snow gets into your spreader and combines with the salt, you may end up with a frozen block of ice inside your machine.

Having spent half her life in the Midwest and the rest in the mountains, Michelle Larson is no stranger to snow or the amount of time it takes to remove it. Because she’d rather spend a little more upfront than buy a tool or appliance twice, she strongly believes in the power of product testing for finding quality items that are meant to last.

#7725. How Does Google Maps Know There’s Traffic Before You Hit It?

A map app can spot a traffic jam before drivers reach it. Here’s how phones detect slowdowns, predict delays, and sometimes get it wrong.

Most drivers know this experience. They’re en route somewhere when their smartphone map app starts pushing back their ETA. Soon, brake lights appear ahead as traffic slows to a crawl.

But how did the navigation app know about the traffic before the driver encountered it? Popular navigation apps like Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze use real-time location data from drivers’ phones to detect slowdowns and estimate traffic conditions.

Learn what’s happening and why the estimates aren’t always right.

Map apps combine location data from many phones to understand traffic conditions on the road. Google explains that it uses combined location data for this, and Waze says drivers share real-time information just by driving with the app open. When enough drivers slow down in the same area, the app can show a backup on the map.

Apps also use past traffic information to predict delays before drivers encounter them. “To predict what traffic will look like in the near future, Google Maps analyzes historical traffic patterns for roads over time,” Google’s wevsite states.

These predictions help apps estimate arrival times and suggest alternate routes when traffic starts building.

“Our predictive traffic models are also a key part of how Google Maps determines driving routes,” the Google website continues. “If we predict that traffic is likely to become heavy in one direction, we’ll automatically find you a lower-traffic alternative. We also look at a number of other factors, like road quality. Is the road paved or unpaved, or covered in gravel, dirt or mud?”

Drivers can also report problems such as accidents and hazards through Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze, though the options vary by app and region. These reports help explain why traffic has slowed down. Google says it also uses data from local governments, which can flag road restrictions such as construction.

The colored lines on the map show where traffic is building. In most navigational systems, green means no traffic delays, orange means medium traffic, and red means delays, with darker red indicating slower speeds.

Traffic updates are generally useful, but they aren’t always accurate. Apple, for example, says it displays incident markers only when it has a high level of confidence in the reports it receives, so a new incident may take time to appear. Coverage also varies depending on how much information the apps receive. On less-traveled roads, fewer drivers may contribute location data, making it harder for apps to detect slowdowns in real time.

Arrival times are estimates, too. Google says its predictions combine historical patterns with live conditions, but it also notes that historical patterns aren’t always reliable indicators of what the road will look like. Conditions can also change unexpectedly because of events like snowstorms.

Map apps can help drivers avoid delays, but their estimates aren’t guaranteed. Drivers still need to follow road signs and pay attention to the conditions around them.

#7723. We Tested Home Generators to Find the Best Picks for a Power Outage

By Glenda Taylor, Austin Fracchia, Mark Wolfe, Zach Lazzari

Updated Nov 3, 2026 9:44 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

During a power outage, a home generator can keep the lights on, the HVAC running, and the appliances powered, but there are a lot of options out there, from whole-house to quiet inverter models. Because we’re big on helping our readers navigate the array of products that make life easier, our team tackled the task of testing home generators.

These independent power sources range in output for a variety of needs. After researching more than 40 top models, we selected the highest-scoring models in a range of categories for hands-on testing. Our favorite was the Champion 7500-Watt Dual-Fuel Generator thanks to its versatile operation and multiple outlets.

Whether you’re looking for a generator to run an entire home or to power only a few essentials, you can find a top-notch one in this lineup. Keep reading to find out how each one performed and to learn more about what to consider when shopping for the best home generator for your needs.

Bottom line: Our comprehensive testing reveals top home generators for every need, from budget-friendly to whole-house solutions.

When shopping for a generator, it’s easy to become overwhelmed by the available options on the market. While the following models vary in fuel type, electrical load, and intended use, each one earned a spot on this lineup by excelling in real-world tests.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 5/5

This Champion 7,500-watt dual-fuel generator delivers enough electricity to power up an off-grid jobsite or keep critical home circuits running through a utility outage. It includes numerous convenience features, like a push-button electric starter, covered outlets, and a fold-out transport handle. In our tests, the push-button starter worked perfectly, no matter the weather.

We appreciated its two locking 30A outlets (one 120V and one 120/240V) for powering a home, workshop, RV, or heavy-duty tools like portable welders. It also has four household-style 120V-20A outlets for lower-wattage applications. On a 7.7-gallon tank of gas, this generator supports a 50 percent load for up to 10 hours or up to 5.5 hours with a 20-pound propane cylinder. Using propane, we ran a portable table saw, miter saw, router, and air compressor for 4 hours and had just under half a tank of propane left over.

On the downside, its heavy weight made it tough to navigate across a yard and lift in and out of a truck. It also does not include an idle controller, which leads to more fuel consumption than eco-throttle-equipped generators. Still, it offered plenty of power and access points for the price.

Get the Champion 7500-watt home generator at Blain’s Farm & Fleet.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Power 4.5/5; Portability 5/5; Noise 4/5; Value 4.5/5

A no-frills dual-fuel generator that’s small enough to tuck away in the corner of a garage or in a truck bed, the Pulsar 2200-watt generator delivered an easy experience powering our test equipment. The 1.18-gallon generator can run for up to 8 hours on half load on a single tank of gas.

Setting up the generator for the first time was fairly straightforward, though filling the oil for the first time proved to be a challenge. The side panel that we needed to unscrew and pop off to access the oil fill port and dipstick was difficult to remove. We also had to lay the generator on its side to fill it with oil, which required a bit of balancing as it’s not completely flat. Balancing while pouring oil was a bit tricky, to say the least. Starting it was a piece of cake. Turning on the Pulsar requires pulling a recoil start, but the engine kicked on after just a couple of pulls—even in the cold.

We used several appliances, including a couple of heat guns and hair dryers at the same time to test the generator at different loads. As promised, the generator handled a combined 1,800 watts without much issue and shut power off when we overloaded it with 2,300 watts.

The Pulsar’s noise level seemed louder than expected, but it was still in a reasonable range for its output. It’s a great option for budget-priced backup power for light-duty power needs such as small DIY projects and powering a couple of household appliances during an outage.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

It’s hard to beat Westinghouse’s 4,500-watt inverter generator for power output, versatility, and portability. It’s not the highest-wattage model we tested, but it excelled at running several power tools, including grinders and saws, as well as the essentials in our travel trailer. Setting it up was a snap—all we had to do was add oil and fill the gas tank. Best of all, it’s quiet and efficient.

While this would be a great emergency generator, we also think it’s a top-notch pick for RVs, camping, and remote powering due to its quiet and efficient operation.

The iGen4500 has a 3.4-gallon gasoline tank that can run up to 18 hours. Since it’s an inverter, it only burns enough to cover the appliances or tools it’s powering. This makes it more eco-friendly than noninverter models that burn fuel at a set rate no matter how much power is being drawn. This backup generator offers a variety of power ports, including a 30A port, two 20A ports, and two USB ports. However, it weighs almost 105 pounds without fuel, so lifting it up and down can be challenging for one person.

Read our full review: Westinghouse iGen4500 Inverter Generator

Get the Westinghouse home generator at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 4/5

The Honda EU2200i inverter generator offers reliability, simple operation, and low noise. Honda estimates that the EU2200i runs at 48 to 57 weighted decibels, and we found that its sound easily gets lost in the background. It comes equipped with a Honda GXR120 commercial series engine that delivers 120 volts and up to 1,800 running watts and 2,200 starting watts. A 125V-20A duplex outlet allows users to plug in two electrical cords without worrying about overloading the generator. T

his machine is compatible with the Honda My Generator mobile app for remote monitoring and is parallel-ready for use with a second Honda EU2200i (connection kit sold separately). It also features a built-in carbon monoxide sensor and safety shutoff. In two separate tests, we used the Honda generator to power a full-size refrigerator for 4 hours and then a portable table saw and miter saw for an 8-hour workday. We even added a USB hub to charge a phone and laptop.

In each test, the devices worked perfectly, the electrical current remained strong and steady, and the breaker didn’t trip. The generator’s molded plastic handle is well placed, and when combined with the machine’s proportions, the unit is fairly easy to carry, even though it weighs nearly 50 pounds. We would have appreciated a built-in USB port in addition to the wall-style outlet, though. As it was, we had to unplug a tool that draws 10A just to charge a device using less than 3A.

Still, a clean electrical current and quiet operation in a lightweight, easy-to-stow package make the Honda an excellent choice for a home backup generator.

Get the Honda home generator at Amazon or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Power 5/5; Portability 4/5; Noise 4/5; Value 4.5/5

Westinghouse WGen9500DF is an all-around top pick when the power goes out. It has a 6.6-gallon gasoline tank that will keep it running for 12 hours at 25 percent load and up to 8 hours at 50 percent load. (Actual tank runtime may vary depending on gasoline quality and electrical load.) With a 20-pound propane tank, the generator will run up to 7 hours at 50 percent load.

This is a heavy model, weighing 211 pounds, but it mainly came assembled—all we had to do was attach the wheels and the handle. We tested it first with gasoline, followed by propane, and the results were excellent with both fuels. We ran several power tools simultaneously and powered an oven/range and a clothes dryer (at separate times). A nice perk was the remote fob, which allowed us to start the generator from 90 feet away.

The WGen9500DF is a good pick for those who want an emergency generator to power more than just a couple of cell phones.

Get the Westinghouse home generator at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 3.5/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 5/5

A distinct downside with fuel-powered generators is the inability to run them indoors due to hazardous fumes. Power stations, however, can be used indoors to power several appliances and electronic items, depending on their capacity. The Generac GB2000 is a beefy power backup that provides up to 1,600 running watts of electricity and comes with three standard outlets, four USB ports, and a 12V DC car port. Charging the GB2000 took about 3.5 hours when we plugged it directly into a standard AC outlet.

We also charged it with solar panels, but the day was slightly overcast, which kept it from charging quickly—it took about 5 hours to charge from 28 to 100 percent. A sunnier day or stronger solar panels would likely have charged it more quickly. When fully charged, we used it to run our fridge, a miter saw, lamps, a laptop, and cell phone—not all simultaneously. We made about 20 cuts with the miter saw and noticed no lag in the saw’s power. It took a couple of hours to fully charge the cell phone by placing it on the wireless charging panel at the top of the GB2000.

We left the fridge and laptop plugged in for several hours without depleting the battery—we still had 20 percent when we unplugged them. The Generac is well suited as an emergency backup for essential appliances or a remote power source for tailgating and camping, but at 43 pounds, it’s a bit heavy if you plan to carry it very far on trails.

Get the Generac home generator at The Home Depot or Walmart.

Before testing, we carefully researched more than 40 portable and standby generators and over a dozen high-capacity power stations. We looked at consumer satisfaction, ease of use, price, and versatility. We also considered brand reputation—manufacturers like Champion, Honda, Westinghouse, and Briggs & Stratton are highly respected in the generator industry.

Our goal was to pinpoint models that would suit diverse user needs. This list includes powerful, gas-fueled, and dual-fueled generators in addition to quieter inverters and even solar power stations.

Team members assembled and fueled the generators using the appropriate fuel types. Then we plugged in power tools, home appliances, and electronic devices to see if the generators would produce the advertised wattage. We used an online wattage calculator to help us estimate the correct wattage for testing. In addition, we took note of the noise the generators produced when operating (some models are quieter than others), and we took portability into account.

For each generator, we awarded points based on quality and performance. At the end of testing, we averaged the points to determine which models were best suited to specific applications and users.

Several factors can affect each type of generator’s overall functionality when the power goes out. Keep the following considerations in mind when searching for the best home generator to keep you powered up when severe weather or a natural disaster causes an outage.

Finding the best generator for your power needs involves weighing the four types available. Each type has its own set of pros and cons, and one is likely to suit your home’s specific needs better than the others.

Home standby generators, also called whole-house generators, are large, permanently installed generators that connect to a home’s electrical panel for backup power during an electrical outage. They are equipped with an automatic transfer switch (explained in later sections) that automatically switches on the generator’s power supply when it detects a loss of utility power. Home standby generators are most commonly powered by natural gas or propane, but some diesel models are available.

Home standby generators have the largest power ratings and are usually, though not always, powerful enough to satisfy the electrical demands of an entire home. They can power utilities such as water heaters and central air conditioners. The downside is that they’re the most expensive to purchase and install and require installation by certified professionals. An electrician is needed to connect it to the electrical panel, and a plumber may be required to connect the propane or natural gas line to the generator.

As the name suggests, portable generators are small and can be moved to different locations. Compared to standby options, these are cheap home generators. They can have a wide range of power output ratings. Some may only power a limited number of electrical items and appliances, while large-capacity portable generators may have a 30A outlet for connecting a transfer switch.

Many options are gas-powered generators, but some are powered by diesel or propane. Multifuel generators (dual- and tri-fuel) are powered by multiple fuel sources, including gasoline, diesel, propane, and/or natural gas. Be advised that fuel-powered generators should never be used indoors since the engine can emit a toxic level of CO, leading to sickness or death.

Inverter generators are technically a type of portable generator, but they offer a different set of pros and cons. As opposed to conventional generator engines that constantly operate at the same output rate, inverter generators adapt to power demand.

This makes them more fuel efficient, allowing them to have smaller fuel tanks and more portability than other generators. This efficiency reduces their CO emissions. It also makes them quiet generators, usually only producing around a 60-decibel noise level—the same volume level as a typical conversation.

All of these advantages make them a popular choice among campers and RVers who value silent operation and portability. The disadvantages? Inverter generators are typically more expensive than regular portable generators and generally produce less power.

Portable power stations are essentially battery banks that store electrical power. Instead of using gasoline, diesel, propane, or natural gas, power stations are charged in a standard electrical outlet or via solar panels. Solar-powered power stations are often called solar generators and offer a practically unlimited and renewable power source—just as long as the sun is shining.

These power stations are usually designed to be compact and lightweight for incredible portability. They are also virtually silent when in operation. In addition, they can be safely used indoors since they don’t produce any harmful emissions.

The primary disadvantages are that they’re usually more expensive than conventional portable generators and have significantly lower power output. That being said, they can be used to power a handful of essential appliances during an outage.

A generator’s size equates to the amount of power in watts it can generate, ranging from 800 to greater than 50,000-watt power capacity. Generators are sized in both “peak watts” (also called “starting watts”) and “running watts,” but the running watts rating reveals how many continuous watts the generator can supply to keep the electricity running to the connected items. Peak watts are the number of watts the generator can produce for a few seconds to satisfy the extra demand from starting motor-driven items like power tools.

The running watts rating dictates the number of electrical appliances you can run simultaneously and for how long. Because a generator’s starting watts can be 1,000 to 2,000 watts greater than its running watts, it’s important to understand the difference when determining your home’s power requirements.

To determine the generator size you need, calculate the total number of watts your most essential electrical items consume. All electrical appliances are required to have a label that displays their wattage rating; you simply need to add together the wattage figure listed on each item you want to power during an electrical outage.

Generally speaking, a refrigerator consumes between 700 and 1,200 watts; a window air conditioner consumes around 1,000 watts; a portable space heater consumes about 1,500 watts; and lights can be anywhere between 60 and 600 watts. Most households typically require around 5,000 watts to power the most essential components.

A transfer switch connects a generator to a home’s main electrical panel and allows you to switch, or “transfer,” between grid power and generator power. There are both manual and automatic transfer switches. Manual transfer switches require you to physically switch over the power at your electrical panel when the power goes out, while an automatic transfer switch automatically switches over power from the grid to generator power when it detects a loss of power.

Generators can be equipped with various features that make their operation as convenient as possible. These include:

Along with the various features that contribute to convenience, there are also a few important safety features that many generators incorporate into their design, particularly with regard to CO detection. These include:

Operating a generator isn’t complicated, but there are a few tips you’ll want to keep in mind to ensure effective and safe operation and avoid any harm to yourself or your generator when the power goes out.

First of all, it’s important to use extension cords that are sufficiently powerful. As a general rule, use at least 12-gauge outdoor-rated electrical cords for larger appliances (like refrigerators) and at least 14-gauge cords for everything else. Cord length is also a concern since the voltage drop from cords that are too long can damage or destroy the appliances they’re supplying. Although you’ll want to keep a portable generator outside and away from your home, remember not to exceed a 100-foot extension cord length.

When running a home generator, it’s best to keep it on a level surface. If a generator is placed on a slope or hill, the internal lubrication system could malfunction and lead to premature engine wear and damage. Finally, ensure the generator has cooled down before you refill it since spilling gasoline on a hot engine can cause a fire.

Since generators can be both lifesaving and expensive, it’s natural to have some questions before you’re confident in your decision. To this end, consider the answers to these frequently asked questions. Together with the above shopping considerations, these answers provide you with just about everything you need to know about emergency power generators.

Most municipalities and towns require that you have a permit before a standby generator is installed. However, not all locations have this requirement. Check with your local zoning authority to find out if a permit is required in your community.

To determine the necessary power rating for your generator, add up the wattage of all the appliances you want to run during an electrical outage. As a general rule, a generator should have at least a 5,000-watt capacity to power a home’s essential appliances. But, your home could require substantially more power than that.

Yes, fuel-powered home generators require oil to operate properly without wearing out the moving parts.

Most manufacturers recommend that the whole-house generator be installed at least 5 feet from doors, windows, vents, and any flammable material. There may also be local regulations about the placement of a whole-house generator, so make sure to check local guidelines to ensure that your whole-house generator meets local building codes and installation guidelines.

No. A generator should not be plugged into a house outlet because it is both dangerous and illegal in many locations. This is called backfeeding and it can severely damage the home’s electrical system or even cause a fire. Additionally, any technicians who are working on electrical lines on the same power grid are at increased risk of electrocution.

You can connect a generator to individual appliances using a series of extension cords, or if you want direct power for entire circuits in the home, have a standby generator professionally installed.

On average, it will take an experienced technician about 1 to 2 full days to complete the installation of your whole-house generator. It could take 1 to 2 weeks to prep for the installation, such as pouring a concrete pad and running the wires connecting the generator to the electrical panel.

The exact lifespan depends on the specific product, but in general, the overall lifespan of a whole-house generator is about 1,500 to 3,000 hours.

#7722. Accusing University Lecturer Who Called Police of "Blatant Racial Profiling" Leads to $37,500 Defamation Verdict

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

You can see the verdict form, from Thursday, here. The jury had asked whether they could suggest additional remedies besides the money:

But the court referred the jury to Instruction No. 10, which focused solely on monetary damages.

The backstory, from the opinion this April Judge Rebecca Pennell (E.D. Wash.) in Riera v. Central Wash. Univ., which let the case go forward:

Mr. Riera was employed in a fixed term, non-tenure track faculty at Central Washington University (CWU)…. On the morning of April 1, [2024,] Mr. Riera called the CWU police to report an older, "apparently homeless," woman wandering around Samuelson Hall. He said he wanted to make a report "before things get … out of control." An officer reported to Samuelson Hall and confirmed the identity of the woman as a CWU professor. No further action was taken by campus police or Mr. Riera.

The CWU professor shared her experience with two colleagues. The colleagues immediately filed bias complaints with CWU, alleging the target of Mr. Riera's call—a Black woman—had been the victim of racial profiling.

This led to a great deal of institutional response, including a discussion at a faculty senate meeting. Defendant Erdman, "a lecturer at CWU and member of the faculty senate, emailed unofficial minutes [of the meeting] to non-tenured faculty," and her notes included this:

Without naming names or describing the incident, [CWU President] Wohlpart expressed his outrage at a recent unconscionable incident on campus.

From my own knowledge, I think I can tell you the basics: It was an incident of blatant racial profiling. Campus police were called because a person of color was sitting quietly in the lobby of a CWU building for a brief interval. The person turned out to be a highly distinguished faculty member—but was compelled to produce and show ID before being left in peace.

(I must remark that this is outrageous on multiple levels. All CWU buildings are public; they belong to the State of Washington and its people. Anyone may sit in the lobby of any of our buildings. There was no reason at all to call the police—except, I guess, that this was a person of color.)

Wohlpart called the incident "unacceptable" and said that Central is working to see to it that such a thing doesn't happen again on our campus….

Riera sued Erdman, among others, and the court allowed his defamation claim to go forward in part:

[M]ost of [Erdman's] statements cannot be characterized as false. The only exception is Defendant Erdman's statement that what happened on April 1 "was an incident of blatant racial profiling." A jury could conclude this statement falsely asserts that the person who called police on April 1 engaged in intentional racial profiling. And, given widely-shared public records revealed Mr. Riera as the caller, a jury could also conclude Defendant Erdman's statement was about Mr. Riera.

Defendants argue that regardless of truth or falsity, Defendant Erdman's statement cannot be considered defamatory because it falls under the common interest privilege. "The common interest privilege applies with the declarant and the recipient have a common interest in the subject matter of the communication." The privilege applies to "persons involved in the same organization, partnerships, associations, or enterprises who are communicating on matters of common interest." Examples include officers of a nonprofit association or partners to a partnership. The privilege arises "when parties need to speak freely and openly about subjects of common organizational or pecuniary interest." …

If the privilege exists, it can be lost in two circumstances (1) if the speaker is not acting in the ordinary course of their work or (2) the speaker's statement was made with actual malice; i.e., reckless disregard for the truth. Whether the privilege has been lost under either scenario is a question of fact.

Here, the parties appear to agree that members of CWU's faculty senate are members of the same organization who share a common interest. The dispute lies in whether an exception applies.

The Court concludes there are issues of fact regarding whether Defendant Erdman's statements fell outside the scope of the privilege. Going to the first exception, Defendant Erdman had no official responsibility for taking notes at faculty meetings and she was not required to share her notes with other members of the senate faculty. A jury could therefore conclude that her statements were outside the ordinary course of her work as a member of a senate.

With respect to the second exception, Defendant Erdman was not a witness to the April 1 incident and no investigation had yet taken place. A jury could therefore conclude Defendant Erdman was reckless in asserting that the call to CWU police was an act of blatant racial profiling…. [T]he allegations against Defendant Erdman raise questions of fact that must be resolved by a jury.

Note that the court granted summary judgment as to plaintiff's defamation claim against President Wohlpart; as to plaintiff's defamation claim against CWU, the court stated that "Mr. Riera appears to have abandoned this claim and the summary judgment briefing does not describe how CWU as an institution may be liable for defamation." The one remaining defendant at trial was Erdman.

UPDATE 11/3/26 4:45 pm: I had originally written that the claims against the University were abandoned, but apparently plaintiff's counsel is disputing that, and intends to appeal the court's dismissal of the claims against CWU and Wohlpart. I've revised the post to say that the court stated the claim was abandoned.

NEXT: City's Using Meta Moderation Assist Feature for Facebook Comments Doesn't Violate First Amendment

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. #7721. Don’t Get Caught Off Guard by the First Frost Again — Bookmark This Checklist for Next Year

From HVAC systems to roofs and paint cans, these simple maintenance tasks can prevent big-ticket repairs.

In years past, when I’ve failed to prep my home for the first frost, I’ve ended up with burst garden hoses, broken tree limbs and cars that won’t start. But sometimes, procrastinating on winterizing a home can lead to even more severe problems, including foundation damage and burst pipes.

“If you want to save money and protect your pocket book, then jump on the winterization of your home and yard,” says home improvement expert Todd Tripp. “Before the first frost is also an excellent time to put your yard and equipment to sleep, so that it will start fresh for you in the spring.”

Ahead, Tripp and other experts walk through exactly what to do before the first frost of the season.

Water that accumulates around a home during winter can cause foundation damage as it freezes and thaws. Before the first frost comes, clean leaves and other debris from the gutters and downspouts, check for leaks and extend downspouts so they carry water at least 10 feet away from the house.

Common mistake: “Don’t clean the gutters too early in the fall, before nearby trees have finished shedding their leaves,” says remodeling expert Michael DiMartino.

Many outdoor water systems fall victim to the first freeze, bursting as the water inside of them expands into ice. To prevent this:

“It’s also a good idea to put the hoses and other garden equipment in a shed, so they’re covered and out of the elements,” says Tripp.

Freezing water can split plumbing pipes. Then, once temperatures rise, the water leaking out can cause significant damage. To prevent this, use foam insulation sleeves, insulation tape or heat tape around pipes that run through unheated areas, such as garages, crawls spaces, basements, attics and exterior walls.

“Also, look for gaps around windows, doors, foundations and where pipes enter the home, and seal them properly, since cold drafts can make vulnerable plumbing even more susceptible to freezing,” says plumber Tim Fancher. As a bonus, this will also help keep mice and spiders out.

Pro-tip: know where your main water shutoff is, says Fancher. If a pipe does burst, quickly shutting off the water will help mitigate damage.

Frost can cause weak trees limbs to fall, potentially damaging your roof or car, so trim trees before the winter season begins. That will also keep dead leaves from accumulating on your roof.

While you’re at it, prune shrubbery and cut back perennial plants. “Before the frost comes is also a good time to put in your winter fertilizer,” says Tripp. “Blend on your lawn and in your flowerbeds so that it will percolate down into the soil over the winter.”

Cracks or damaged seals can let in moisture, which will cause further damage, plus invite cold drafts. Before the first frost, caulk any gaps and fix damaged weather stripping. “This will also save you a lot of money on your heating bill, plus keep moisture and mold out of your house,” says Tripp.

Also, fogging between your window panes is often a sign that the window seal has failed, and the window may not be insulating your house as well as it once did, says DiMartino.

Any damage to your roof will likely get worse once temperatures drop. Before the first frost, visually inspect your roof for missing, loose or damaged shingles and signs of water intrusion. Also, check the attic for moisture.

Pro-tip: “If you notice moisture in the attic or leaks in the home’s living spaces, it could be a sign that the roof needs to be repaired or replaced,” says DiMartino.

A freezing evening is no time to have the furnace fail. That could lead to burst pipes and even jeopardize your family’s safety. Home improvement expert Eric Goranson recommends hiring a pro to inspect your system every year, plus tune it for maximum efficiency.

While you’re at it, don’t forget to winterize your air conditioning system. “It’s not completely necessary to cover the outside condenser unit, but it’s a good practice to cover it or wrap it to protect it from frost,” says Tripp.

Safety check: Before using your furnace or fireplace in the fall, check your chimney for debris like spiderwebs and bird nests, which could cause it to not vent properly, or even catch on fire.

Cold weather can reduce your battery’s cold cranking amps, making it hard to start on the first cold morning, says Goranson. Before the first frost, test your battery, check your tires and windshield wipers and bring other neglected maintenance up to date.

Pro-tip: Run a Top Tier fuel through your vehicle at least once a month. “Those have cleaners in them that help keep your engine’s fuel system clean,” says Goranson.

Drain fuel or put fuel stabilizers in gas-powered lawnmowers, trimmers and blowers, before stowing them in the shed. “The best trick I was ever told, which has worked for over 30 years, is to drain the fuel out of your landscape equipment, then start it up and let it run until it’s completely out of gas,” says Tripp. “That gets all the fuel out of your carburetor so that it does not varnish or gum up, and it will start in the spring every time.”

For electric-powered equipment, charge the batteries to the manufacturer-recommended levels, then leave them in a temperature-controlled space.

If your garage isn’t insulated, chances are there are items in there that won’t fare well when temperatures drop. Especially check the storage instructions on paints and other liquids, plus battery-powered equipment. Also, don’t forget to check the seals on your garage door.

Pro-tip: Move shovels and ice melt to a place where they’re easy to access, leave a clear walking path through the garage and designate somewhere to put wet boots and tools, says garage expert Alan Bernau Jr. “You want to be able to use the garage in winter, not just cram everything into it,” he says.
